name: The Hierophants of Set (Wolves at the Door)

text.content:
Source: Libellus Sanguinis III: Wolves at the Door, Book Three: Serpents

Greatest of the seven surviving Hierophants who rule the Followers of Set in the great god's absence, Nakhthorheb is called the First Son, said to be of the same tribe as Set himself. He holds the Hierophants together through sheer force of will and the implicit threat of the god's wrath, and though all commands issued to the clan must be agreed upon by all seven elders, it is Nakhthorheb from whom such edicts spring. He regards all Cainites as evil and all non-Egyptians as little better than animals, and since the loss of Tanis has grown ever more suspicious and wary, spending many nights wandering the wastes of Lower Egypt as Set himself once did, and planning the restoration of Egypt's glory.

Source: Libellus Sanguinis III: Wolves at the Door, Book Three: Serpents

Second in power among the Hierophants, Seterpenre was in ages past a mighty sorcerer who served the elders of Set's tribe. Unlike Nakhthorheb, he is far more tolerant of outsiders, favoring alliances with other Cainites when they serve the purposes of Set — it was he who architected the Setites' early alliance with the Tremere, an act that cost him dearly in Nakhthorheb's eyes. Seterpenre continues to push the Hierophants to direct Setite influence outward, beyond Egypt's borders and into the West.

Source: Libellus Sanguinis III: Wolves at the Door, Book Three: Serpents

Said to have been Set's concubine in ancient times, Maatkare is the mortar between the stones of Hierophant unity, reminding her fellow elders of their holy purpose. Her beauty is said to be great enough to stop the heart of a strong man. Outwardly devoted to none but her lord and god, she nonetheless builds consensus among the Hierophants and holds influence over them that may exceed even Nakhthorheb's or Seterpenre's; nothing happens among the elders from night to night without her approval, though she has offered no plans or initiatives of her own. Her true motives remain as mysterious as the face of the moon.
